1
INTEREST OF AMICUS CURIAE1
The Florida Association of Court Clerks, Inc. d/b/a
Florida Court Clerks & Comptrollers (“FCCC”) is a
nonpartisan, nonprofit, voluntary association whose
membership includes each of the sixty-seven clerks of
the circuit and county courts (“Clerk(s) of Court” or
“Clerk(s)”) throughout Florida.  There is a Clerk of Court
for each of Florida’s sixty-seven counties.  Clerks of Court
are Florida constitutional officers and are an integral part
of the Florida state court system.
Pursuant to Florida statutes, the Clerks of Court are
responsible for jury management for Florida courts.  As
such, the Clerks of Court organize and process prospective
jurors and the jurors selected, and pay all costs related
to jury management.
The question presented in this case is whether
Williams v. Florida , 399 U.S. 78 (1970),  should be
overturned, thereby increasing the size of juries in
Florida’s non-capital criminal cases from six to twelve
m e m be rs.   Th e  C o urt’ s  d ecis i o n  ma y  ul tima te l y  h a v e  a
direct and substantial impact on Florida’s court system
including jury management and court administration.
Because Clerks of Court are the Florida officials charged
with jury management, every Clerk of Court within the
state of Florida, and thus every member of the FCCC,
could be greatly affected by the decision.  Therefore, the
FCCC and its entire membership have a great interest
in the outcome of this case.
1. No party or party’s counsel authored this brief in whole
or in part or made a monetary contribution intended to fund the
preparation or submission of the brief.

2
SUMMARY OF ARGUMENT
A primary purpose of stare decisis  is to foster the
predictable development of legal principles so that they
may be safely relied upon.  The doctrine requires courts
to stand by precedent so that people and organizations
can plan their actions and practices accordingly without
fear of sudden changes in legal rules.
The reliance that the Florida state court system,
including the Clerks of Court, has placed in the fifty-six
year old holding in Williams that six-person juries are
constitutional for non-capital criminal cases is substantial.
If Williams is overruled, thousands of cases that are
currently in process or that are on direct appeal would
potentially have to be retried.  There is also the possibility
of post-conviction challenges to convictions.  Any retrials
or proceedings resulting from a reversal of precedent
would involve the expenditure of enormous amounts of
resources.
Further, overturning Williams to require twelvemember juries in all criminal trials would place an immense
strain on an already heavily burdened court system by
prolonging the duration of the proceedings.  Additionally,
an overturning would greatly impact Florida’s Clerks of
Court’s administrative and financial capability to handle
jury management.  A concern for resources for jurors
and jury management has always been at the core of
Florida’s six-person system.  If Williams is overruled, jury
management costs could essentially double.  Overruling
Williams would also require considerable renovation and
addition to the physical infrastructure of courthouses and
their premises in many Florida jurisdictions.

3
Given the circumstances, in its stare decisis analysis, it
is appropriate for the Court to consider the long-standing
reliance interests that Florida’s court system and Clerks
of Court have in Williams.  Because of the meaningful
reliance, the Court should decline to overrule Williams.
ARGUMENT
I.  THE DOCTRINE OF STARE DECISIS SUPPORTS
RETENTION OF THE PRECEDENT SET FORTH
IN WILLIAMS v. FLORIDA.
The doctrine of stare decisis  provides that “today’s
Court should stand by yesterday’s decisions.”  Kimble
v. Marvel Entm’t, LLC, 576 U.S. 446, 455 (2015).  The
doctrine is “a foundation stone of the rule of law.”  Id.
(quoting Michigan v. Bay Mills Indian Cmty., 572 U.S.
782, 798 (2014)).  Stare decisis  is the “preferred course
because it promotes the evenhanded, predictable, and
consistent development of legal principles, fosters reliance
on judicial decisions, and contributes to the actual and
perceived integrity of the judicial process.”  Id. (quoting
Payne v. Tennessee, 501 U.S. 808, 827 (1991)).
Stare decisis  requires something more than a good
argument that the Court wrongly decided an issue.
Kimble, 576 U.S. at 455.  Even in constitutional cases,
overturning precedent requires “special justification.”
Gamble v. United States, 587 U.S. 678, 691 (2019) (quoting
Arizona v. Rumsey, 467 U.S. 203, 212 (1984)).  Such special
justification requires more than “ambiguous historical
evidence” before the Court will “flatly overrule” its major
decisions.  Id.  (quoting Welch v. Texas Dep’t of Highways
& Public Transp., 483 U.S. 468, 479 (1987)).

4
This Court has considered several factors in
determining whether to overrule established precedent,
including the quality of the prior decision’s reasoning, the
workability of the rule it established, its consistency with
other related decisions, developments since the decision
was handed down, and reliance on the decision.  Janus
v. Am. Fed’n of State, Cnty., and Mun. Emps., Council
31, 585 U.S. 878, 917  (2018).  In particular, the Court
has consistently identified the absence of a meaningful
reliance interest as a factor supporting overruling.  E.g.,
Payne, 501 U.S. at 827; Kimble, 576 U.S. at 457; Ramos v.
Louisiana, 590 U.S. 83, 107-08 (2020); Nat’l Republican
Senatorial Comm. v. Fed. Election Comm’n, 146 S. Ct.
2404, 2424 (2026).
As set forth below, not even including the other
states that would be directly affected by the overruling
of Williams, the reliance interest that the Florida court
system alone has in this Court’s precedent is immense
and weighs heavily against overruling and in favor of
preserving the decision.
A.  Florida Has a Strong Reliance Interest in the
Williams v. Florida Decision.
1.  The Reliance Interest Is Greater than that
Considered by the Court in Ramos.
In Williams v. Florida, the issue of whether Florida’s
six-person jury system was constitutional was presented
to this Court.  Williams, 399 U.S. at 86.  And this Court
clearly and unequivocally held that Florida’s system
was constitutional.  Id. at 103.  As might be anticipated,
this ruling of constitutionality by the nation’s high

5
court engendered substantial and reasonable reliance.
“[R]eliance upon a square, unabandoned holding of the
Supreme Court is always justifiable reliance….”  Quill
Corp. v. N. Dakota, 504 U.S. 298, 321 (1992) (Scalia, J.
concurring) (emphasis in original), overruled on other
grounds by South Dakota v. Wayfair, Inc., 585 U.S. 162
(2018).  Accordingly, with complete and total confidence in
and reliance on the Court’s pronouncement, in the fifty-six
years that followed the ruling, many thousands of cases
were tried under the law that permitted six-person juries
for non-capital crimes.
Such reliance has been reinforced by this Court for the
past fifty-six years.  See, e.g., Minor v. Florida, 146 S. Ct.
1668 (2026) (denying petition for writ of certiorari asking
Court to reconsider Williams); Parada v. United States,
146 S. Ct. 1477 (2026) (same); Cunningham v. Florida,
144 S. Ct. 1287 (2024) (same); Pretell v. Florida, 143 S.
Ct. 1027 (2023) (same); Khorrami v. Arizona, 143 S. Ct.
22 (2022) (same); Davis v. Florida, 143 S. Ct. 380 (2022)
(same); Phillips v. Florida, 142 S. Ct. 721 (2021) (same);
McDonald v. City of Chicago, 561 U.S. 742, 868 (2010)
(“the Court has repeatedly declined to grant certiorari” to
review Williams) (Stevens, J., dissenting); United States
v. Gandin, 515 U.S. 506, 510 n.2 (1995) (twelve-person
jury “is not an indispensable component of the right to
trial by jury”); Collins v. Youngblood, 497 U.S. 37, 52 n.4
(1990) (“the Court’s holding…that the Sixth Amendment
requires a panel of 12 persons is…obsolete”); Holland
v. Illinois, 493 U.S. 474, 478 (1990) (Sixth Amendment
requires “use of a jury numbering at least six persons”);
Batson v. Kentucky, 476 U.S. 79, 85 n.6 (1986) (“jury of six
persons is not unconstitutional”); Brown v. Louisiana, 447
U.S. 323, 330 (1980) (citing Williams for its holding that

6
“six-person jury does not violate Sixth and Fourteenth
Amendments”); Burch v. Louisiana, 441 U.S. 130, 134-
35 (1979) (stating that in Williams, “the Court held that
this constitutional guarantee of trial by jury did not
require a State to provide an accused with a jury of 12
members and that Florida did not violate the jury trial
rights of criminal defendants charged with nonpetty
offenses by affording them jury panels comprised of only
6 persons”); Crist v. Bretz, 437 U.S. 28, 37 (1978) (federal
requirement of 12 jurors does not bind States); Ballew v.
Georgia, 435 U.S. 223, 230 (1978) (a jury of six does not
violate the Sixth and Fourteenth Amendments); Ludwig
v. Massachusetts, 427 U.S. 618, 625 (1976) (a jury of twelve
is not required in order that the central purpose of the
jury trial requirement is served); Taylor v. Louisiana,
419 U.S. 522, 528 (1975) (stating that Court had rejected
challenge that use of six-person juries in non-capital
criminal cases violates the Sixth Amendment); Colgrove
v. Battin, 413 U.S. 149, 151-52 (1973) (citing the holding
in Williams that six-member juries are constitutional in
certain criminal cases and affirming denial of petition for
writ of mandamus to direct respondent to impanel twelveperson jury in federal civil trial); Dunn v. Louisiana, 399
U.S. 520 (1970) (dismissing appeal of appellate decision
denying pretrial motion for twelve-person jury).
Currently, as the State of Florida has stated in its
brief, approximately 5200 criminal convictions that were
tried before six-person juries are on direct appeal.  Brief
for Respondent at 35.  See Edwards v. Vannoy, 593 U.S.
255, 262 (2021) (“A new rule of criminal procedure applies
to cases on direct r e vi e w ,  e v e n  if  th e  d e f e n d an t’ s  trial
has already concluded.”) (emphasis in original) (citing
Griffith v. Kentucky , 479 U.S. 314, 328 (1987)).  This

7
number does not include those cases presently being
tried.  It also does not include the possibility of postconviction collateral challenges if Williams is overruled.2
Certainly, overturning the long-standing precedent of
Williams would potentially impose an enormous burden
on Florida’s court system.  See United States v. Mechanik,
475 U.S. 66, 72 (1986) (“The reversal of a conviction entails
substantial social costs:  it forces jurors, witnesses, courts,
the prosecution, and the defendants to expend further
time, energy, and other resources to repeat a trial that
has already once taken place….”).
In Ramos, the Court ruled that the Sixth Amendment
right to a jury trial, as incorporated against the States by
way of the Fourteenth Amendment, requires a unanimous
verdict to convict a defendant of a serious offense.  The
Court’s ruling abrogated the Court’s previous decisions
in Apodaca v. Oregon, 406 U.S. 404 (1972), and Johnson
v. Louisiana, 406 U.S. 356 (1972).  In overturning these
prior decisions, the Court considered the reliance interests
of Louisiana and Oregon, the only two States that at
that time did not require a unanimous jury verdict for
the conviction of a criminal defendant.  The Court found
that these States had minimal reliance on the Court’s
precedent.  Ramos, 590 U.S. at 107-08.  The Court stated
that neither Louisiana nor Oregon claimed “anything like
the prospective, economic, regulatory, or social disruption
litigants seeking to preserve precedent usually invoke.”
Id. at 107.  The Court noted that the reliance interests
asserted “in only two States” involved retrying felony
2. “As long as retroactive application on collateral review
remains a real possibility, the crushing burden that this would
entail cannot be ignored.”  See Ramos, 590 U.S. at 160 (Alito, J.,
dissenting).

8
convictions still on direct appeal “somewhere in the
hundreds.”3   Id.  This was characterized as “a modest
number of retrials.”  Id. at 115 (Sotomayor, J., concurring
in part).  In acknowledging that the retrials would “surely
impose a cost,” the Court discussed its ruling in Booker
v. United States, 543 U.S. 220 (2005), in which the Court
held that the Federal Sentencing Guidelines are advisory
rather than mandatory and vacated and remanded nearly
800 criminal cases for resentencing.  Id. at 108.
In the case at bar, the consequences would be much
more severe.  If Williams is overturned, the potential
number of retrials would be far greater than the several
hundred acknowledged in Ramos.4  And the tsunami of
possible retrials implicated in Florida does not include the
affected cases in the other states that since Williams have
utilized juries in criminal cases with fewer than twelve
j ur o rs .   Th e  P e ti ti o n e r  h as  i d e n tifi e d  s ix  o th e r  s ta te s
that utilize juries of fewer than twelve members when
the crime charged is a felony.  Brief of Petitioner at 13
(in addition to Florida, identifying Arizona, Connecticut,
Indiana, Louisiana, Massachusetts, and Utah).  The
Petitioner does not discuss sizes of juries in other states,
but it appears that many other states allow juries of fewer
than twelve to consider some types of criminal cases.
Barbara Luppi & Francesco Parisi, Jury Size and the
3. The Court cited to the amicus brief filed by the State of
Oregon stating that for the pertinent period two-thirds of the
673 felony jury trials in Oregon would have had a non-unanimous
verdict and that at most the cases remaining on direct appeal
“may” surpass a thousand.  Id. at 108, n. 68.
4. Also, resentencing as mandated by the Court in Booker
does not involve the resources required for retrials.

9
Hung-Jury Paradox, 42 J. Legal Stud. 339, 402 (2013)
(“A total of 11 states currently use juries composed of
fewer than 12 jurors in felony and misdemeanor trials”
and “[a]n additional 29 states allow juries of fewer than
12 in misdemeanor cases … [t]his brings the number of
states that allow smaller juries in some criminal cases to
40.”) (citing Bureau of Justice Statistics 2004).
Misdemeanor cases may potentially constitute
“serious crimes” as that term has been defined by this
Court. 5  Thus, “the reliance here is not only massive; it is
concrete.”  Ramos, 590 U.S. at 161 (Alito, J., dissenting).
2.  Florida Has an Interest in Alleviating
Strain on Its Court System.
Florida also has a substantial interest in the strain
an increase in jury size would place on its already heavily
burdened court system.  Florida currently relies on
Williams to further its stated goal “to secure the speedy,
and inexpensive determination of every proceeding.”  See
Fla. R. Gen. Prac. & Jud. Admin. 2.110.  Increasing jury
size to twelve in all non-capital criminal cases would
greatly hinder this goal.
Pursuant to the Florida Supreme Court’s Panel
Size Guidelines (“Panel Guidelines”), the jury panels
of prospective jurors for criminal trials would at least
5. Codispoti v. Pennsylvania, 418 U.S. 506, 512 (1974) (“ our
decisions have established...those crimes carrying a sentence of
more than six months are serious crimes and those carrying a
sentence of six months or less are petty crimes.”).  See Fla. Stat.
§ 775.082(4) (individuals convicted of a misdemeanor of the first
degree may be sentenced to a jail term of up to one year).

10
double in size if juries are increased from six to twelve
members.6  Based on the six-member jury system, for
most criminal trials the current Panel Guidelines provide
for a panel of from fourteen to twenty-two.7  However, for
twelve-member jury trials, the Guidelines provide for a
panel of forty.8
With jury panels that would at least double, the time
spent in voir dire, reviewing personal data, and qualifying
and impaneling a jury could increase substantially.9  Jury
deliberation time would be expected to increase with a
twelve-member jury,10 as well as hung juries.11  This means
that the duration of criminal trials could increase, leading
to a delay in court processing times and the scheduling
of other trials.
6. In re:  Jury Management System, Fla. Admin. Order
No. AOSC06-13 (June 9, 2006) https://flcourts-media.flcourts.gov/
content/download/645601/file/sc06-13.pdf
7. Id.
8. Id.
9. See Edward Thompson, Six Will Do!, 10 Trial 6, at 14
(Nov.–Dec. 1974); New Jersey Criminal Law Revision Comm’n,
Six-Member Juries , at 2-4 (1971); Andrew W. Bogue & Thomas
G. Fritz, The Six-Man Jury, 17 S.D.L. Rev. 285, 288 (1972); Hon.
Lloyd L. Wiehl, The Six Man Jury, 4 Gonzaga Law Review, 35,
40-41 (1968); Hon. Richard H. Phillips, A Jury of Six in All Cases,
30 Conn. B. J. 254, 356-57 (1956).
10. Bogue & Fritz, supra n. 9, at 288; Wiehl, supra n. 9, at
40; Thompson, supra n. 9, at 12.
11. Adam M. Chud & Michael L. Berman, Symposium:
Communicating With Juries: Six-Member Juries: Does Size
Really Matter?, 67 Tenn. L. Rev. 743, 752 (Spring 2000).

11
The negative consequences of any extended court
processing time of criminal cases are many, 12 and one
such consequence is the detrimental effect on criminal
defendants.13  Thus, any additional burden on the criminal
justice system caused by increased jury panels and sizes
could have a negative effect on Florida’s promise of a
“speedy and inexpensive determination” of criminal cases
to which defendants are entitled.
3.  The Impact on Jury Management Is a
Significant Factor in Florida’s Reliance
Interest.
Additionally, here, any reliance analysis should include
the impact on Florida’s administrative and financial
capacity to handle jury management.  Previously, this
Court acknowledged a State’s interest in jury size.  Ballew,
425 U.S. at 243-44.  While the Court in Ballew found no
significant State interest in the reduction of jurors from
six to five, the Court acknowledged a substantial interest
12. See Douglas Evans, The Waiting Game: How Lengthy
Court Case Processing Times Keep Jail Populations High,
CUNY Inst. for State & Loc. Governance (Feb. 3, 2026), at 2-4;
Sam Zarkower, Expanding the Courts to Reduce Case Backlogs,
Cornell J. Law and Pub. Pol’y (Nov. 10, 2021), at 1-2.
13.  Consequences of extended court processing time
for criminal cases include extended jail time that can cause
employment, financial, family and relationship disruption,
along with mental and emotional distress.  Evans, supra note
12; Zarkower, supra n. 12.  Individuals on pretrial release
are also subject to interference in their financial and personal
circumstances.  Evans, supra n. 12.  Prolonged proceedings can
also increase the incentive to make a guilty plea or accept a less
than optimal plea deal. Id.; Zarkower, supra n. 12.

12
in the reduction of jurors from twelve to six.  Id.14  Indeed,
the jury management element of Florida’s reliance
interest in a six-member jury for non-capital criminal
trials is substantial.
For over 149 years, beginning in 1877, Florida has
used six-person juries for non-capital criminal trials.  In
1874, the Florida Constitution was amended to permit
the Florida Legislature to set jury size.  Art. VI, § 12,
Fla. Const. (amended 1874) (“The number of jurors
for the trial of causes in any court may be fixed by
law.”).15  Subsequently, on February 17, 1877, the Florida
Legislature approved a statute reducing the jury size from
twelve to six to try all offenses not capital, and all civil
causes.  Ch. 3010, § 6, Laws of Fla. (1877). 16
Of course, a discriminatory purpose would not be a
valid justification for this practice or for any other rule
14. In making this finding, the Court cited in part to New
Jersey Criminal Law Revision Comm’n, supra  n. 9, at 1-4
(recommending the reduction of the size of juries in all civil and
criminal cases, except capital cases, from twelve members to six
noting the “substantial savings to the judicial system, in time
and expense”); Bogue & Fritz, supra n. 9, at 288-90 (referencing
a survey taken of South Dakota clerks of court to determine jury
expenses and the reduction in expenditures if jury panels were
reduced from twelve to six); William R. Pabst, Jr., Statistical
Studies of the Costs of Six-Man Versus Twelve-Man Juries, 14
Wm. & Mary L. Rev. 326, 328 (1972) (calculating a savings in juror
hours of 41.9% with the reduction to six members).
15. https://library.law.fsu.edu/Digital-Collections/CRC/CRC-
1998/conhist/1874amen.html
16. https://edocs.dlis.state.fl.us/fldocs/leg/actsflorida/1877/1877.
pdf

13
of criminal procedure.  Although the Petitioner points
out that the original rules were adopted during the
Reconstruction era, Florida readopted its constitution
more than ninety years later in 1968 under different
circumstances.  Art. I, § 22, Fla. Const. (“The right of
trial by jury shall be secure to all and remain inviolate.
The qualifications and the number of jurors, not fewer
than six, shall be fixed by law.”).  The Petitioner has made
no effort to show that the 1968 constitution retained the
six-person jury for discriminatory purposes.
Moreover, rather than a discriminatory motive for the
1874 constitutional provision, a historical examination of
the origins of the reduction of the jury size to six indicates
that costs and expenses, not discrimination, were the
concerns in the policy discussions.  Immediately prior to
the adoption of the 1874 constitutional amendment, the
Governor of Florida addressed the Florida Legislature
on the topic of juror costs.  In his annual message to the
Legislature dated January 1, 1874, the Governor stated in
that portion of the message pertaining to “Financial,” that
“[t]he largest and most unsatisfactory source of expense to
the treasury of the State is for jurors and witnesses.”  Fla.
S. Jour., 16 (7th Sess. 1874). 17  Subsequently, on January
4, 1878, the Florida Attorney General reported to the
Governor regarding the last session of the Legislature:
“I believe the administration of justice is secured under
the new system [of six-member juries] as fully as it was
under the old, and certainly at much less expense.”  Fla.
S. Jour., 147 (10th Sess. 1879).18
17. https://www.flsenate.gov/UserContent/Session/Archive/
Journals/1874/1874_Journal_complete.pdf
18. https://www.flsenate.gov/UserContent/Session/Archive/
Journals/1879/147-att_gen_79.pdf

14
Indeed, for nearly 150 years, resources for jury
management have been an ongoing issue and concern
regarding Florida’ s court system.  The Clerks of Court
have many responsibilities pertaining to jury management
and the expenses are considerable.  Florida statutes
require Clerks to maintain lists of potential jurors and
implement and maintain an electronic system for the
purpose of jury venire selection.  Fla. Stat. §§  40.011,
40.02, 40.021, 40.022, 40.221, 40.225.  Clerks must operate
and update their systems in accordance with technical
standards and procedures that are adopted.  Fla. Stat.
§ 40.225.  Clerks must generate and issue summonses to
prospective jurors.  Fla. Stat. § 40.23.  Clerks must pay
jurors and prospective jurors a per diem stipend.  Fla.
Stat. §§ 40.24, 40.32.  Clerks of Court are also responsible
for paying meal and refreshment expenses when a jury is
deliberating or sequestered, as well as the cost of lodging
when required.  Fla. Stat. §§ 40.26, 40.32.
There are also, of course, significant jury-related
administrative and personnel costs appurtenant to these
duties, including for processing and qualifying prospective
jurors against other state databases; reviewing and
resolving requests for excusal, postponement, or statutory
disqualification; managing intake and identity verification;
and conducting and overseeing juror orientation in the
jury assembly rooms.
For the fiscal years 2016-2025, the Florida Legislature
appropriated $11.7 million annually to the Clerks of Court
for reimbursement for these costs.  See Ch. 2025-198,
§ 4, Laws of Fla.19  For fiscal year 2026-2027, the Florida
19. See generally https://flccoc.org/clerks-budget/jury/

15
Legislature increased the appropriation to $16.5 million
to better reflect the actual costs incurred by Clerks.  Ch.
2026-232, § 4, Laws of Fla.  Regardless of appropriations
from the Legislature, Clerks are required to pay the
mandated jury costs in their individual counties and fund
any shortfalls from their existing local budgets. 20
FCCC conducted a poll of its sixty-seven members,
and Clerks of Court for fifty-nine Florida counties,
representing approximately eighty-eight percent of
Clerks overall, responded.21   Of the Clerks responding, for
calendar year 2025, six-person criminal jury trials were
on average seventy-two percent of the total number of
jury trials held. 22   For calendar year 2024, of the Clerks
responding, seventy-three percent of overall jury trials
were six-person criminal jury trials.23  These percentages
varied by county.  For example, of the 749 jury trials held

4.  Renovations and Additions to the Physical
Infrastructure of Florida’s Court System
Would Be Necessary If Jury Size Is
Increased.
The Florida Association of Criminal Defense Lawyers
and the Florida Public Defender Association, Inc. state
in their amicus brief supporting Petitioner that “Florida
is already equipped to return to 12-person juries,” and
that “[r]estoring 12-person juries will not require Florida
to re b uil d i ts co urth o uses. ”  B ri ef f o r Fla. Ass ’ n Crim.
Defense Lawyers, et al. as Amicus Curiae  at 23-26.
However, the reality is that an increase to twelve-person
juries in all criminal trials would require considerable
renovations and additions to the physical infrastructure
of Florida’s court system in many individual jurisdictions.
Florida has had six-person criminal juries for all
non-capital crimes since 1877.  All of Florida’s still active
courthouses were built after this date.  And the FCCC
poll reflects that, not surprisingly, many Florida counties
have courtrooms built to accommodate only six person
juries. 33  By way of example, in Broward County, sixty
courtrooms are built to accommodate only six-person
juries.34  In Duval County, thirty-nine courtrooms are built
for six-person juries, and in Pinellas County, twenty-four
courtrooms.35  The number of courtrooms not equipped for
twelve-person juries is substantial and varies by county.
Likewise, several Clerks reported that the courthouses

court system.  In this regard, it is appropriate for the Court
to consider such disruption in its stare decisis  analysis.
